name: UMAP map of dictionary directions
summary: A scatter of every dictionary direction from several autoencoder runs at once, projected to a plane so that features whose decoder vectors point in similar directions land together. It is read only for which points clump with which — the two axes have no units and no meaning — and it is the paper's picture of feature families and of coarse features sitting inside the finer ones they split into.
explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

The claim in this part of the paper is about geometry, not behaviour: that the families the authors found by *reading text* — base64 features, Arabic script features — are also families in the 512-dimensional space of MLP activations, with small angles between their dictionary vectors ([[feature-geometry-clusters]]). And that a coarse feature from a small dictionary sits among the finer ones that split out of it as the dictionary is widened ([[feature-splitting]]).

The tabular version is a pairwise cosine-similarity matrix over twenty thousand directions, which nobody reads. A mean cosine similarity inside each named family answers a narrower question: it needs the family list up front, so it can only score groups already named, and can never show that unnamed clumps exist. A bar chart per family drops the part actually being argued — that the clumps of *different* [[dictionary-learning-run]]s sit inside one another. What the argument needs is one picture of a whole dictionary at once, in which "these belong together" is visible without deciding in advance which points to compare. That forces a neighbour-preserving projection.

The cost is real, and the paper does not hide it: [[umap]] will draw clusters out of almost any input, so this shape corroborates families found by reading text rather than establishing them on its own.

### How to read it, step by step

Every dot is a direction, not an activation. Each learned [[feature]] owns one column of the decoder matrix $W_d$ ([[dictionary-decoder]]) — the [[feature-direction]] it writes into the 512 neuron activations of the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]] whenever it fires. Those columns are the points. How often a feature fires, and how hard, plays no part. Columns are held at unit length ([[unit-norm-dictionary-columns]]), so magnitude carries nothing and angle is the only comparison left; both embeddings are fit with `metric="cosine"`, `n_neighbors=15`.

Read the axes as nothing at all. No units, no scale, no fixed orientation. Only co-location is information: two dots together mean two dictionary vectors at a small angle. Do not read the gap between two blobs as a distance, and do not read position — a blob on the left is not more of anything.

Colour is the run, meaning the width of the [[sparse-autoencoder]] ([[expansion-factor]]). Look first at whether the coarse run's markers sit *underneath* knots of the finer runs rather than off in a region of their own; then at the labelled families; then at the outlying island of [[ultralow-density-cluster]] features and [[dead-neurons]], which the paper reads as artifacts of autoencoder training and excludes elsewhere.

### What a bad result would look like

The families scattered. Arabic script features landing in three unrelated places with unrelated features in between, base64 features spread through the bulk — then conceptually similar features do not have small angles, and whatever clumps the picture does show are UMAP's own doing rather than the dictionary's.

For the splitting claim, the failure looks different: the coarse markers gathered in their own corner, the fine ones elsewhere. That would say a wider dictionary learns *different* directions rather than finer versions of the same ones, and the reading of dictionary size as a zoom level ([[dictionary-resolution]]) would be gone.

Even a clean picture leaves two things open. Clumps with no label attached are not evidence of anything. And because the method manufactures structure, the strongest fair phrasing for a good-looking map is "consistent with", not "shows".

### Where it comes back

Fig-1 is the interactive version, embedding A/0's 512 and A/1's 4,096 features together, $4{,}608$ points, `min_dist=0.05`. Colour there does no work: the payload is the list beside the map, human-written labels grouped by [[hdbscan-feature-clustering]] run on a separate 10-dimensional UMAP so that flattening to a plane does not decide the groups, and ordered by [[one-dimensional-umap-ordering]]. Ids follow the paper's [[feature-notation]], and A/0 and A/1 ids mixing inside one cluster is the splitting claim in list form.

Fig-44 is the static version and adds A/2's 16,384 features, with `min_dist=0.01`, so clumps pack tighter and read as solid. Here colour does carry the run, which is what makes coarse-under-fine visible; two knots are named by arrow, and the ultralow-density and dead region is pushed off to one side.
